text:
## Results

All recommendations below achieved panel consensus agreement as being appropriate, and these recommendations should be considered extensions or additions to recommendations made in the initial international consensus guidance. The range outside of the “appropriate” category (7–9) indicates the breadth of opinions (dispersion) within the panel.

### Thymectomy

The multicenter, randomized, rater-blinded trial of thymectomy in MG (MGTX) enrolled patients younger than 65 years with AChR-positive (AChR-Ab+) generalized nonthymomatous MG of <5 years duration. Sixty-six subjects underwent extended transsternal thymectomy and received prednisone using a standard dosing schedule, whereas 60 subjects received the standardized prednisone dosing schedule alone. An effect favoring thymectomy was seen in both of the coprimary outcome measures: reductions in the time-weighted average quantitative MG (QMG) score and the time-weighted average alternate-day prednisone dose. Secondary outcome measures, including azathioprine use, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) use, and hospitalizations for MG exacerbations, also favored thymectomy plus prednisone. Benefits were seen within the first year and were sustained through year 3. In a post hoc analysis, neither the prednisone dose nor QMG scores were significantly different between the 2 treatment groups in patients 50 years or older. An extension of the MGTX trial followed 68 (61%) participants from the original trial for 2 additional years. At 60 months, lower time-weighted average QMG scores and a reduction in average time-weighted prednisone dose favored thymectomy plus prednisone. A recent AAN Practice Advisory recommended that clinicians should discuss thymectomy with patients with AChR-Ab+ generalized MG and should counsel patients considering minimally invasive thymectomy techniques that it is uncertain whether the benefit attained by extended transsternal thymectomy will also be attained by minimally invasive approaches (level B).

#### Recommendations

1. a. In nonthymomatous, generalized MG patients with AChR-Ab, aged 18–50 years, thymectomy should be considered early in the disease to improve clinical outcomes and to minimize immunotherapy requirements and the need for hospitalizations for disease exacerbations (median 9, range 2–9). b. Thymectomy should be strongly considered in patients with AChR-Ab+ generalized MG if they fail to respond to an initial adequate trial of immunotherapy or have intolerable side effects from that therapy (median 9, range 5–9).
2. Thymectomy for MG is an elective procedure and should be performed when the patient is stable and deemed safe to undergo a procedure where postoperative pain and mechanical factors can limit respiratory function (median 9, range 8-9).

Recommendations 4 and 5 below are unchanged from the 2016 consensus guidance.

1. Endoscopic and robotic approaches to thymectomy are increasingly performed and have a good track record for safety in experienced centers. Data from randomized, controlled comparison studies are not available. Based on comparisons across studies, less invasive thymectomy approaches appear to yield similar results to more aggressive approaches (median 9, range 4–9).
2. Thymectomy may be considered in patients with generalized MG without detectable AChR-Ab if they fail to respond adequately to immunosuppressive (IS) therapy or to avoid/minimize intolerable adverse effects from IS therapy. Current evidence does not support an indication for thymectomy in patients with MuSK, low-density lipoprotein receptor–related protein 4, or agrin antibodies (median 9, range 6–9) (table e-3, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

### Ocular MG

A small RCT comparing prednisone with placebo in patients with 11 ocular MG who had previously failed to achieve minimal manifestation (MM) status after 4–6 weeks of pyridostigmine found that 5 of 6 participants (83%) in the prednisone group achieved the primary end point of sustained MM status at a median of 14 weeks on prednisone (median dose 15 mg/d), compared with none of 5 in the placebo group. Three of the 5 placebo participants switched to prednisone (60 mg/d) with rapid taper; 2 attained sustained MM status. A prospective cohort study of 13 consecutive ocular and 76 generalized MG patients evaluated the effect of IS agents on ophthalmoparesis. Fifty-nine percent of patients had complete resolution of ophthalmoparesis within 12 ± 2 months of initiation of IS agents. Patients with milder ophthalmoparesis had greater odds of symptom resolution in the first year of treatment. Median time to resolution was 7 months after IS agents were started.

Evidence for the efficacy of thymectomy in ocular MG is limited by the retrospective design of most published studies. In a case-control study of 47 patients with nonthymomatous ocular MG who underwent thymectomy matched to 67 patients who refused surgery, there was no difference in the proportion of patients achieving stable remission at a median follow-up of 100–116 months. A retrospective analysis of 236 patients with thymomatous and nonthymomatous MG reported no improvement after thymectomy in 25 patients, of whom 17 (68%) were ocular or predominantly ocular, over 12 months of follow-up. In another retrospective case series of 52 patients with MG, only 2 of 11 patients with ocular MG (18%) achieved remission after thymectomy, in contrast to 28%–50% of patients with generalized MG.

A retrospective case series of 110 patients with ocular MG who underwent extended transsternal thymectomy reported that at a median follow-up of 33.5 months, 26% achieved complete remission (defined as asymptomatic without medications for 12 months). Five patients had a thymoma. A retrospective case series of 49 nonthymomatous ocular MG and 12 ocular MG with thymoma undergoing thymectomy followed for a mean duration of 9 years reported a cure defined as asymptomatic without the need for medications in 51%. In yet another retrospective case series of transcervical thymectomy in MG, 57% of 12 patients with ocular MG achieved MGFA postintervention status (PIS) of complete stable remission (CSR) at 5 years. A subsequent case series of 151 patients with MG who underwent transcervical thymectomy followed for 5 years showed a higher odds ratio for remission in ocular MG compared with generalized MG without controlling for other variables (analysis performed by P.N.). In 12 patients with ocular MG undergoing thymectomy because of an abnormal chest CT scan, all but one required additional immunosuppression after thymectomy; 6 achieved remission at a mean follow-up of 81 months. In a retrospective analysis of 50 patients with juvenile MG undergoing thymectomy, of whom 46% were ocular, 50% showed improved PIS at a mean of 3.5 years of follow-up. There was no difference between ocular and generalized MG. In a meta-analysis of 26 studies of thymectomy in nonthymomatous MG, the pooled CSR rate was 0.51. There was high heterogeneity in the meta-analysis model, indicating substantial differences among the included studies.

#### Recommendations

1. Ophthalmoparesis or ptosis in ocular MG that is not responding to anticholinesterase agents should be treated with immunosuppressant agents if symptoms are functionally limiting or troublesome to the patient (median 9, range 7–9).
2. Corticosteroids should be used as the initial IS agent in ocular MG. Steroid-sparing IS agents may be needed when corticosteroids alone are ineffective, contraindicated, or not tolerated (median 9, range 6–9).
3. Data from a single small RCT suggest that low-dose corticosteroids may be effective for ocular MG and may avoid side effects associated with high-dose corticosteroids (median 9, range 4–9).
4. AChR-Ab+ patients with ocular MG who do not respond adequately to acetylcholinesterases and who either prefer not to take IS therapy or have contraindications to or are refractory to IS agents may be offered thymectomy (median 8, range 5–9) (table e-10, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

### Rituximab

Most studies of RTX are retrospective, and some combine patients with AChR-Ab, MuSK-Ab, and seronegative MG. A multicenter blinded prospective review of MuSK-Ab + MG patients demonstrated that 14 of 24 (58%) patients treated with RTX achieved MM status and required only low-dose IS therapy, compared with 5 of 31 (16%) of the non-RTX group.

In a prospective open-label study of 22 refractory AChR-Ab+, MuSK-Ab+, and seronegative MG, MG manual muscle testing (MMT) scores revealed significant improvement from baseline at a mean follow-up of 29 ± 19 months in the AChR-Ab+ and MuSK-Ab+ groups. Another prospective open-label study of 14 patients with refractory AChR-Ab+, MuSK-Ab+, and seronegative MG reported improvement in MMT scores at a mean follow-up of 22 months. The time to peak response after a single cycle of RTX was 4.5 ± 1 months. A retrospective multicenter study of MuSK-Ab + MG reported that RTX given in the dose of 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks and then monthly for the next 2 months was associated with lower relapse rates (18%) compared with a regimen of two 1 g infusions separated by 2 weeks (80%). A retrospective Austrian nationwide study of 56 patients with AChR-Ab+ and MuSK-Ab + MG reported that 26% of patients were in remission 3 months after treatment with varying dosing protocols of RTX. At a median of 20 months, 43% were in remission and 25% achieved MM status. A single-center retrospective study of 21 AChR-Ab+, 3 MuSK-Ab+, and 4 patients with double-seronegative MG found that muscle strength improved significantly from baseline at 6 months and then stabilized up to 36 months, and PIS was improved in 43% at 6 months. A retrospective combined analysis of previously published case reports of 169 patients between January 2000 and August 2015 reported that 72% of MuSK-Ab + MG and 30% of AChR-Ab+ MG patients treated with RTX achieved MM status or better. The number of cycles of RTX varied but did not have an effect on the response. A recent systematic review of previous studies of 165 patients with AChR-Ab+ MG treated with RTX concluded that despite heterogeneous outcome measures, significant clinical improvement was seen in 113 patients (68%), with 36% achieving remission. A phase II RCT of RTX (Beat-MG) enrolled 52 patients with generalized nonthymomatous AChR-Ab+ MG on a stable regimen of prednisone for 4 weeks or prednisone plus another IS agent for 6 months. Two cycles of RTX 6 months apart were compared to placebo with the primary outcome being a steroid-sparing effect (≥75% reduction in mean daily prednisone requirements in the 4 weeks before week 52 compared with the 4-week period before randomization). The study was designed to assess futility (nonsuperiority). Preliminary results reported that the area under the curve for prednisone was not significantly different between RTX and placebo groups, with 60% on RTX and 56% on placebo achieving the primary outcome. There were no significant differences in mean QMG or MG-composite (MGC) changes between the groups. The study suggests that in mildly to moderately symptomatic generalized AChR-Ab+ MG, RTX is unlikely to have a clinically meaningful steroid-sparing effect over 12 months.

Three cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy have been reported in MG. One was RTX related, although the patient had previously received other IS agents, another patient was on azathioprine and prednisone, and the third patient was on prednisolone, IVIg, and azathioprine.

#### Recommendations

Recommendation 1 is unchanged from the 2016 consensus guidance.

1. Rituximab should be considered as an early therapeutic option in patients with MuSK-Ab+ MG who have an unsatisfactory response to initial immunotherapy (median 9, range 4–9).
2. The efficacy of RTX in refractory AChR-Ab+ MG is uncertain. It is an option if patients fail or do not tolerate other IS agents (median 8, range 4–9) (tables e-2 and e-7, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

### Methotrexate

Studies on the use of MTX in MG are limited, and the available data do not provide convincing evidence of efficacy. In a retrospective case series of 16 patients with MG treated with MTX, (abstract only) 8 patients reduced pyridostigmine doses and 6 showed “clinical improvement.” A prospective open-label case series published only as an abstract reported that 14 of 16 patients with MG treated with MTX had an improved PIS on a mean follow-up of 20.6 months. In a single-blinded trial, 24 patients with generalized MG on prednisone were randomized to MTX (11) or azathioprine (13). At 24 months, the average prednisone dose required to achieve and maintain MM status was lower in both MTX- and azathioprine-treated patients but was not different between the groups. At months 10 and 12, the prednisone dose was lower in the MTX group, but the confidence interval includes clinically meaningful and nonmeaningful effects. Similar proportions of both groups achieved MM status, and there were no differences in QMG or MG-activity of daily living (MG-ADL) scores between the groups. An RCT enrolled 50 patients with AChR-Ab+ MG taking prednisone at a dose of ≥10 mg/d. Patients were randomized 1:1 to MTX 20 mg/wk or placebo. There was no difference in the primary outcome measure, the area under the prednisone dose-time curve between months 4 and 12, and the mean 12-month change in QMG, MMT, MG-Quality of life, MG-ADL, and MGC was no different between treatment groups.

#### Recommendation

1. Although evidence from RCTs is lacking, oral MTX may be considered as a steroid-sparing agent in patients with generalized MG who have not tolerated or responded to steroid-sparing agents that are better supported by RCT data (median 9, range 5–9) (table e-2, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

### Eculizumab

Eculizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against the terminal C5 complement molecule. Eculizumab prevents the formation of the membrane attack complex and reduces damage caused by complement-fixing AChR antibodies. In a phase II crossover RCT of 14 patients with refractory generalized AChR-Ab + MG, at the end of the first treatment period, 6/7 (86%) of eculizumab-treated patients achieved the primary end point of a 2-point reduction in the QMG score, compared to 57% with placebo. A repeated measures mixed model of data from all visits revealed significant differences in the QMG score favoring eculizumab. Eculizumab was well tolerated. In a phase III international multicenter RCT of 125 patients with refractory generalized nonthymomatous AChR-Ab+ MG (REGAIN), the primary outcome measure of change in the MG-ADL score from baseline to week 26, measured by worst-rank analysis of covariance, was not significantly different (p = 0.0698) between eculizumab and placebo arms. However, QMG score change on worst-rank analysis of covariance, all prespecified secondary endpoints (changes in QMG, MGC, and MG-QOL15 scores and responder analyses of QMG and MG-ADL scores), and multiple sensitivity analyses showed a significant benefit for eculizumab. Participants who completed the 26-week REGAIN study were followed in an open-label extension (OLE) within 2 weeks of completing REGAIN. A preplanned interim analysis of the OLE at 22.7 months of median follow-up found a reduction in MG exacerbations by 75% compared with the year before REGAIN. In addition, 56% (65/116) of patients achieved MM status or pharmacologic remission. The magnitude of response on all clinical measures for the placebo patients in REGAIN who crossed over to receive eculizumab in the OLE was similar to the eculizumab-treated patients in REGAIN. A clinically meaningful response in MG-ADL and QMG scores was seen in 55% and 39.7% of patients, respectively. Eculizumab was well tolerated. One case of meningococcal meningitis occurred, despite vaccination in the OLE and the patient was successfully treated.

Vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis (both meningococcal conjugate Men ACWY and serogroup B or MenB) is required at least 2 weeks before starting treatment with eculizumab. The conjugate ACWY vaccines available in the United States include Menveo (1 dose, GlaxoSmithKline Biologicals, Inc.) and Menactra (1 dose, single booster 4 years after initial dose if needed, Sanofi Pasteur, Inc.). The 2 brands of MenB vaccine are Bexsero (2 dose series, GlaxoSmithKline Biologicals, Inc.) and Trumenba (3 dose series, Pfizer, Inc.). The brands are not interchangeable, and a course should be completed with the same brand of the vaccine for all doses. The vaccine does not confer absolute protection against meningococcal meningitis. Antibiotic coverage, for at least 4 weeks after immunization, is recommended if eculizumab is started before the 2-week period after vaccination. The recommendations for antibiotic coverage vary. Penicillin VK 250–500 mg every 12 hours is usually the first-line chemoprophylaxis., Erythromycin 500 mg twice daily, azithromycin 500 mg daily, or ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily are alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients. However, both fluoroquinolones and macrolides can worsen MG. Chemoprophylaxis of meningococcal infections in penicillin-allergic patients can therefore be challenging, and infectious disease consultation may be required.

#### Recommendations

1. Eculizumab should be considered in the treatment of severe, refractory, AChR-Ab+ generalized MG (median 9, range 2–9).
2. The role of eculizumab in the treatment of MG is likely to evolve over time. Until further data become available to allow comparisons of cost and efficacy with other treatments, eculizumab should be considered after trials of other immunotherapies have been unsuccessful in meeting treatment goals (median 9, range 5–9).
3. Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices or other local guidelines regarding immunization against meningococcal meningitis should be followed before treatment with eculizumab (median 9, range 8–9).
4. Future research should include assessment of the duration of eculizumab therapy necessary to achieve and maintain treatment goals, its efficacy in other MG populations (MG with thymoma and seronegative MG), and in other stages of disease (MG crises, exacerbations, and early therapy in nonrefractory AChR-Ab+ MG) (median 8, range 4–9) (table e-2, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

### Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors

Immune checkpoints (ICPs) are most often inhibitory molecules expressed on the surface of T cells, which modulate the immune response and prevent host tissue damage due to uncontrolled responses to foreign or self-antigens. The immune inhibitory cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), and programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) are the best-characterized ICPs and are targeted in cancer immunotherapy. CTLA-4 reduces T-cell activation, competing with CD28 in binding B7 molecules (CD80 and CD86) on antigen-presenting cells. PD-1 binds its ligands (PD-L1 and PD-L2) and reduces activated T-cell proliferation through the inhibition of specific phosphorylation pathways., Monoclonal antibodies against CTLA-4, PD-1, and PD-L1 act by blocking these inhibitory ICP molecules to stimulate antitumor immunity (immune checkpoint inhibitors [ICIs]). These include the CTLA-4 inhibitor ipilimumab, PD-1 inhibitors pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and cemiplimab, and the PDL-1 inhibitors atezolizumab, durvalumab, and avelumab. Because of the upregulation of the immune response, multisystem immune-related adverse events (irAEs) such as skin rash, thyroid dysfunction, pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, nephritis, hypophysitis, and neurologic disorders including MG have been reported in patients receiving checkpoint inhibitors.

The literature on irAEs of these drugs is rapidly evolving. De novo MG has been reported in patients treated with anti–CTLA-4 agents (ipilimumab), PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab or pembrolizumab), and with combined (anti–CTLA-4 plus anti–PD-1 or PD-L1) therapy. The estimated frequency of MG among patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors ranges from 0.12% to 0.2%. Exacerbation of preexisting MG and subclinical AChR-Ab+ MG has been reported in patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors.,,

MG onset or exacerbation varies in severity and generally occurs in the early phase of treatment. MG can overlap with other immune-mediated peripheral and central neurologic syndromes., In a review of the literature combined with a single-center experience, of 63 patients with MG due to ICIs, 52 had new-onset MG and 11 had a flare of preexisting MG. Most received PD-1 therapy. Concurrent myositis was diagnosed in 24 patients (37%) and myocarditis in 5 (8%); 2 had the triad of MG/myositis/myocarditis. Median time from ICI initiation to developing MG was 4 weeks (6 days–16 weeks). Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation occurred in 29 patients (45%). Patients with MG/myositis/myocarditis developed respiratory failure more frequently than those with MG alone (54% vs 42%). AChR-Ab titers were elevated in 37/56 (66%) of tested patients. Three patients had AChR-Ab when tested before ICI initiation and antibody titers increased at least 2-fold after ICI initiation. Intravenous corticosteroids were used in 59 of 63 patients. Thirty-eight patients received steroids as first-line therapy and 24 (63%) improved. Four patients with ocular MG developed respiratory insufficiency after corticosteroid treatment. MG symptoms completely resolved in 12 patients (19%), improved in 34 (55%), and worsened in 16 (26%). In a review of 1834 patients receiving ICIs, 4 had MG, of whom 1 was AChR-Ab+. Three were associated with myositis. Three patients with MG received combined CTLA-4 and PD-1 ICIs and one received a CTLA-4 ICI. Concurrent occurrence of MG with myocarditis and thyroiditis was also noted. The diagnosis of ICI-related MG can be challenging. Many patients with cancer have fatigue or generalized weakness. The recognition of the underlying neuromuscular disease may be delayed by the focus on the oncologic illness. Concurrent myositis may make MG difficult to diagnose especially when associated with ocular and bulbar weakness. Seronegative MG appears to be more frequent in these patients, making the diagnosis even more challenging. The severity of the illness may be the result of multiple concurrent conditions including MG, myositis, and myocarditis. CNS involvement may occur in conjunction with MG or MG-myositis overlap. Corticosteroid therapy appears to result in favorable outcomes.

#### Recommendations

1. The risk of MG and other immune-mediated neurologic illnesses should be discussed with patients who are candidates for ICIs (median 9, range 5–9).
2. At this time, there is no evidence to either support or refute the utility of AChR antibody testing in patients without MG before starting ICIs (median 8, range 7–9).
3. MG associated with ICIs is generally severe, with a high rate of respiratory crises (median 8, range 5–9).
4. Preexisting MG does not constitute an absolute contraindication to the use of ICIs, at least in patients with well-controlled disease (MM status or better). However, in these patients:
 - • It may be prudent to avoid combined therapy (anti–CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monoclonal antibodies), given the higher potential for severe irAEs.
 - • Close clinical monitoring, particularly of respiratory and bulbar function, is mandatory.
 - • Although the therapeutic response to ICIs seems to be less satisfactory in patients receiving immunosuppressants, MG treatment should be maintained and may even be restarted in patients whose MG is in remission before treatment with ICIs (median 8, range 5–9).
5. Early aggressive treatment with high-dose steroids in combination with plasma exchange or IVIg may be required in patients who develop overt MG while on ICIs. The decision to withdraw ICIs is determined by the oncologic status (median 8, range 7–9) (table e-9, doi:10.5061/dryad.6hdr7sqxx).

identity_evidence: Source Introduction at line 11: A conventional lipoma is a benign neoplasm composed predominantly of mature adipocytes, usually circumscribed by a delicate capsule or pseudocapsule and situated in the subcutaneous plane. ## Introduction

A conventional lipoma is a benign neoplasm composed predominantly of mature adipocytes, usually circumscribed by a delicate capsule or pseudocapsule and situated in the subcutaneous plane. Most lesions are slow-growing, mobile, and painless, and their softness may become more apparent when the adjacent muscle is relaxed. Although trunk, shoulder girdle, neck, and proximal extremities are common sites, lipomas can arise wherever adipose tissue is present, including the hand, foot, parotid region, larynx, gastrointestinal tract, retroperitoneum, mediastinum, and heart. Parotid lipomas illustrate the anatomic importance of facial nerve relationships even when histology is benign. Head and neck fatty masses include ordinary lipomas, variant lipomas, and liposarcomas, making anatomic localization and imaging-pathology concordance especially important before intervention.

Anatomic behavior depends more on site and depth than on histologic blandness: a small superficial lesion may be inconsequential, whereas a deep lesion may compress muscle, nerve, airway, bowel, or cardiac structures. Fat-containing abdominal and pelvic masses can produce torsion, hemorrhage, obstruction, intussusception, or mass effect and require a broader radiologic differential than a typical cutaneous nodule. Cardiac lipomas are rare but may cause arrhythmia, obstruction, or embolic and compressive phenomena depending on their location. Colonic and duodenal lipomas can become symptomatic through bleeding, gastric outlet obstruction, or intussusception.

The natural history of a conventional lipoma typically involves years of slow, indolent enlargement followed by a period of stability. Pain generally results from pressure on surrounding structures, angiolipoma histology, hemorrhage, or an alternative diagnosis rather than from the expected biology of an ordinary lipoma. Lipomas arising in anatomically confined locations, including the hand, fingers, and toes, may become symptomatic despite relatively small size because the lesion competes for limited space with tendons, digital nerves, blood vessels, and footwear.

The modern World Health Organization (WHO) framework classifies conventional lipoma and atypical lipomatous tumor/well-differentiated liposarcoma as distinct entities rather than sequential stages within a typical malignant transformation pathway. Consequently, new rapid growth, fixation, neurologic deficits, recurrence, or heterogeneous imaging findings should prompt clinicians to reconsider the original diagnosis and pursue appropriate reassessment rather than assuming that a previously diagnosed lipoma has simply developed atypical behavior.

## Treatment / Management

Observation and Intervention Indications

Observation is appropriate for an asymptomatic, clinically classic superficial lipoma when the patient accepts diagnostic uncertainty and understands which changes should trigger reassessment. Reasonable indications for treatment include pain, nerve or tendon compression, restricted motion, airway or gastrointestinal symptoms, recurrent trauma, rapid or continued growth, diagnostic uncertainty, patient distress, and cosmetic preference after shared decision-making. Deep limb lipomatous tumors require more deliberate selection because management depends on imaging certainty, symptoms, anatomic morbidity, and the possibility of atypical lipomatous tumor.

Conventional Excision

Complete marginal excision with submission of the specimen for histopathologic examination represents the standard definitive treatment for a symptomatic or unwanted conventional lipoma. Complete removal generally carries a low risk of recurrence. Before local infiltration or patient positioning alters the anatomy, the clinician should mark the lesion and relevant critical contours. The incision should follow a relaxed skin-tension line while maintaining adequate access for safe dissection. Selection of local anesthesia, field block, regional anesthesia, sedation, or general anesthesia should reflect lesion size, depth, location, anticipated procedure duration, comorbidities, and patient preference.

During excision, the surgeon should incise the capsule and develop the appropriate tissue plane using controlled blunt and sharp dissection. Tethering septa should be divided under direct visualization while named nerves and blood vessels remain protected. When diagnostic certainty remains incomplete, removal of the mass intact helps preserve the specimen for accurate pathologic evaluation. Meticulous hemostasis should follow dissection, with selective irrigation as appropriate.

Dead space can be managed with layered sutures or compression, while drains should generally be reserved for unusually large cavities or anatomic locations at high risk of seroma. Any concerning area should be oriented and specifically communicated to the pathologist. Fragmentation of a large or atypical mass can interfere with assessment of tumor heterogeneity and margins, potentially limiting diagnostic accuracy.

A superficial, well-characterized lesion can frequently undergo removal in an office or ambulatory setting. Deep, intramuscular, recurrent, facial-nerve-adjacent, hand, neck, retroperitoneal, mediastinal, cardiac, or suspected sarcoma lesions require a setting equipped with appropriate imaging, anesthesia, pathology, and rescue capabilities. In a surgical series comparing ordinary lipoma with atypical lipomatous tumor, recurrence occurred substantially more often with atypical lipomatous tumor. Older age, a lesion measuring at least 10 cm, extremity location, and prior resection increased the likelihood that a fatty mass warranted surgical oncology evaluation. When final pathology produces an unexpected diagnosis, clinicians should avoid reflexive reexcision. Expert pathology review, postoperative imaging when indicated, and interprofessional sarcoma discussion should first address residual disease, the biopsy or excision tract and scar, margins, and anticipated morbidity.

Scar-Sparing and Debulking Techniques

Minimal-scar segmental extraction through a limited incision has been reported in a series of 122 procedures, but careful case selection is essential because visualization and intact specimen removal are limited. The squeeze-delivery method is most successful for small, mobile, encapsulated subcutaneous lesions in favorable anatomic sites and is less suitable for fibrous, deep, recurrent, or diagnostically uncertain masses. Small-incision approaches that preserve superficial retaining ligaments or use a 2.5-cm access incision can improve cosmesis for selected large subcutaneous lipomas in experienced hands. A peri-eyebrow incision can conceal a forehead scar, but the dissection corridor must respect the supraorbital and supratrochlear neurovascular structures and confirm that the lesion is truly benign. A 2025 report describing 101 minimally invasive excisions in familial multiple lipomatosis shows technical feasibility for a high lesion burden, but a case report cannot establish superiority over standard excision.

Liposuction and laser-assisted lipolysis can reduce incision length or debulk multiple lesions, including selected facial or large lipomas, but may leave capsule, create contour irregularity, and fragment the diagnostic specimen. A 1,444-nm Nd:YAG laser series reported minimally invasive lipoma management, but device-based evidence remains limited and does not replace histologic assessment when any red flag is present. Multiple-lipomatosis surgery can combine strategic incisions and tunneling to improve aesthetics, although the risks of incomplete removal, hematoma, and sensory injury must be balanced against the scar burden.

Nonsurgical and Condition-Specific Management

Injection lipolysis with deoxycholate has reduced the size of some small superficial lipomas in limited studies. However, formulations, dosing, injection geometry, follow-up protocols, and adverse-event reporting remain nonstandardized, and treatment remains off-label for lipoma. A small study evaluated intralesional triamcinolone acetonide at a concentration of 40 mg/mL for symptomatic subcutaneous lipomas. Corticosteroid injection does not represent standard therapy and can produce lipoatrophy, dyspigmentation, telangiectasia, infection, and incomplete response. Because no medication has an approved and reliably curative indication for lipoma, clinicians should avoid extrapolating cosmetic injection protocols outside a clinical study or appropriately governed specialist practice.

Management of multiple symmetric lipomatosis may involve surgery or liposuction directed toward airway compromise, swallowing dysfunction, impaired movement, neuropathy, and contour concerns. Diffuse, unencapsulated disease commonly recurs, while associated alcohol-related, metabolic, hepatic, and neurologic comorbidities require parallel evaluation and management. Dercum disease requires symptom-centered management that may incorporate pain medicine, rehabilitation, psychological support, sleep care, metabolic health interventions, and selective excision or liposuction of dominant painful nodules. Available evidence remains low quality, and no single therapy has demonstrated reliable curative efficacy.

Symptomatic colonic lipomas arise from the colonic submucosa and may require surgical treatment or advanced endoscopic approaches, including unroofing, dissection, loop-assisted resection, or other techniques selected according to lesion size, morphology, location, associated complications, and endoscopist expertise (see Image. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy of a Lipoid). A duodenal lipoma associated with hematemesis, melena, iron-deficiency anemia, or active hemorrhage requires initial management according to standard principles for upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

[그림/Figure] Figure 3 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy of a Lipoid. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showing a sessile polypoidal lesion in the second part of the duodenum, most likely a lipoma. Contributed by S El-Nakeep, MD

Management includes hemodynamic stabilization, blood count and coagulation assessment, medication review, and timely esophagogastroduodenoscopy. Ulceration over the subepithelial mass or an exposed vessel may identify the bleeding source. Endoscopic resection can provide definitive hemostasis and tissue diagnosis when the lesion remains pedunculated or otherwise technically suitable for resection. Endoscopic snare resection has been successfully used for selected bleeding duodenal lipomas, but prophylactic stalk treatment, retrieval of an intact specimen, and preparedness to manage perforation or delayed hemorrhage remain important components of procedural planning.

Large, broad-based, periampullary, deeply invasive, diagnostically uncertain, or endoscopically unsafe lesions should undergo referral for advanced endoscopic or surgical management rather than routine polypectomy. Published case reports demonstrate that some broad-based giant gastric lesions can undergo advanced endoscopic submucosal dissection. However, adolescent and otherwise complex cases warrant careful interprofessional selection of the treatment approach. Cardiac, retroperitoneal, and other deep visceral fatty tumors require evaluation by organ-specific specialists and often require tissue diagnosis or definitive resection because imaging overlap with liposarcoma carries greater clinical consequences than the overlap encountered with a classic cutaneous lesion.

text:
## Prognosis

The prognosis of a completely evaluated conventional lipoma remains excellent. Conventional lipomas do not metastasize, typically enlarge slowly, and frequently require no treatment when asymptomatic. In one surgical cohort, ordinary lipomas had a recurrence rate of 0.8%, compared with 22.6% for atypical lipomatous tumors, underscoring the importance of accurate diagnostic classification rather than relying on the nonspecific term “fatty mass.” Recurrence of a conventional lipoma generally reflects incomplete excision, an infiltrative intramuscular border, multiplicity, or an incorrect initial classification rather than aggressive malignant transformation. Deep, low-grade lipomatous lesions require management guided by anatomic location and diagnostic certainty because repeat surgery near major nerves, blood vessels, or muscle compartments can produce greater morbidity than carefully planned initial treatment.

Cosmetic outcomes depend on several factors, including lesion size, the degree of excess skin, incision placement, management of postoperative dead space, and the balance between minimizing scar length and achieving complete, controlled removal. Pain and functional deficits generally improve following removal of a discrete compressive lipoma, particularly when intervention occurs before irreversible nerve or muscle injury develops. Symptoms may persist, however, when discomfort results from a broader pain syndrome rather than direct compression from an individual lesion.

An unexpected diagnosis of atypical lipomatous tumor or sarcoma substantially changes the patient’s prognosis, surveillance requirements, and treatment pathway. Such patients require histology-, anatomic site-, and stage-specific counseling and follow-up through an appropriately experienced sarcoma team. Interprofessional assessment supports accurate risk stratification, selection of definitive treatment, and individualized surveillance based on the specific tumor subtype and clinical context.

text:
## Complications

Untreated superficial lipomas most often remain asymptomatic and do not produce complications. As lesions enlarge, however, pressure, friction, or local nerve irritation can cause tenderness or discomfort. Lipomas arising in anatomically confined sites may interfere with surrounding structures and impair grip, gait, tendon excursion, or joint motion. Head and neck lipomas can distort salivary or facial anatomy, with clinical manifestations varying according to lesion depth and location. Potential symptoms include dysphagia, dysphonia, sleep-disordered breathing, and airway compromise. Visceral lipomas can produce more consequential complications, including bleeding, obstruction, intussusception when serving as a lead point, and compression of adjacent organs.

Excision carries several expected procedural risks, including pain, bruising, infection, hematoma, seroma, wound separation, hypertrophic or conspicuous scarring, contour depression, residual skin redundancy, sensory changes, motor-nerve injury, vascular injury, incomplete removal, and recurrence. Alternative techniques, including limited-incision extraction, liposuction, and injection-based approaches, can introduce additional risks, eg, tissue fragmentation, incomplete pathologic evaluation, residual capsule, fat necrosis, surface irregularity, chemical neuritis, dyspigmentation, and lipoatrophy. Among the most consequential complications from a systems perspective involves unplanned excision of a sarcoma initially mistaken for a lipoma. Such an error can contaminate tissue planes, necessitate wider re-excision, and complicate subsequent efforts to achieve effective local disease control.

Clinicians can reduce preventable harm through risk-appropriate imaging before intervention, referral to an experienced specialist before biopsy when malignancy remains a concern, direct-vision dissection when operating near critical anatomic structures, and submission of excised tissue for histopathologic evaluation. Closed-loop communication and review of final pathology further support timely recognition of unexpected diagnoses and appropriate subsequent management. These measures help minimize procedural morbidity, reduce the likelihood of incomplete or inappropriate treatment, and promote coordinated care when a lesion ultimately proves atypical or malignant.

text:
## Deterrence and Patient Education

There is no proven strategy to prevent a sporadic conventional lipoma, and patients should not be blamed for diet, body weight, or minor trauma. Weight management, limiting harmful alcohol use, and controlling metabolic risk improve general health and may be relevant in multiple symmetric lipomatosis, but they do not reliably dissolve an encapsulated lipoma. Advise against home incision, squeezing, or unregulated injection, as these can result in infection, nerve injury, tissue necrosis, and loss of diagnostic tissue.

Explain the working diagnosis and the residual uncertainty, then use shared decision-making to compare observation, conventional excision, scar-sparing approaches, and the option of specialist review. Patients choosing observation should return for rapid or persistent growth, increasing firmness or fixation, new pain, weakness, numbness, skin ulceration, bleeding, recurrence after removal, or airway, swallowing, gastrointestinal, or functional symptoms. Patients undergoing excision should receive written instructions about medication management, wound care, activity, signs of hematoma or infection, scar maturation, and how and when pathology results will be communicated. Numerous lesions, early onset, a strong family history, macrocephaly, asymmetric overgrowth, neuropathy, or endocrine tumors should prompt discussion of genetics or other specialty assessment rather than repeated isolated excisions alone.

text:
## Introduction

Rhinitis medicamentosa (RM), commonly referred to as rebound congestion, is a condition characterized by inflammation of the nasal mucosa caused by excessive use of topical nasal decongestants. Symptoms of RM may include nasal congestion, runny nose (rhinorrhea), sneezing, nasal itching, and postnasal drip. This type of rhinitis can occur alongside allergic and other nonallergic forms.

To accurately diagnose RM, a thorough patient history and a physical examination are essential. Both clinicians and patients need to recognize that certain medications can lead to rhinitis. Despite warnings on prescriptions and manufacturer labels about the potential for dependence associated with some nasal decongestants, drug-induced rhinitis often goes undiagnosed. Increasing awareness of this condition is crucial for achieving more accurate diagnoses and effective treatment. Ideally, the offending medication should be discontinued or replaced.

RM is classified as a subset of drug-induced rhinitis specifically caused by the prolonged overuse of topical nasal decongestants, which leads to a distinct mechanism of congestion. Histological analysis of the sinus mucosa in cases of RM typically shows ciliary loss, damaged epithelium, infiltration of inflammatory cells, and edema. The nasal mucosa may appear swollen and erythematous, with punctate bleeding and minimal mucus production.

Topical decongestants are typically used to relieve nasal congestion associated with allergic rhinitis, acute or chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps, or upper respiratory tract infections. The earliest nasal decongestants were primarily derived from ephedrine, and reports of rebound congestion after prolonged use were common. This phenomenon was observed to develop as early as 3 days and as late as 4 to 6 weeks of use. However, with the emergence of modern vasoconstrictors, such as the imidazoline derivatives, the risk of developing rhinitis medicamentosa appears lower than with earlier generations of nasal decongestants, though it remains clinically significant with prolonged or inappropriate use.

text:
## Treatment / Management

The primary treatment for rhinitis medicamentosa is discontinuation of the topical nasal decongestant. Clinicians should advise patients that nasal congestion may temporarily worsen after stopping the medication; this rebound effect should not be mistaken for treatment failure. Intranasal corticosteroids have been shown to alleviate rebound congestion in animal studies and in several small human trials, and clinicians often use them during the withdrawal period. Additional therapies may include short courses of oral corticosteroids (eg, prednisone at 0.5 mg/kg daily for 5 days), oral antihistamines, corticosteroid injections into the inferior turbinate, oral adenosine, and mast cell–stabilizing agents.

Using nasal saline irrigation as an adjunctive measure may improve symptoms and reduce medication use, particularly for patients with frequent rhinitis. Oral decongestants like pseudoephedrine can provide temporary relief during withdrawal, although supporting evidence is limited, and these agents may worsen symptoms. Patients should be advised of potential cardiovascular contraindications to decongestants. In clinical practice, gradual tapering strategies, such as discontinuing the topical decongestant in 1 nostril at a time or diluting the medication with saline, followed by slow withdrawal, have been shown to be effective.

## Prognosis

The key to successful treatment depends largely on prevention and patient education. Rhinitis medicamentosa typically demonstrates a favorable prognosis when managed appropriately, particularly with discontinuation of the offending topical decongestant. Symptoms generally improve following cessation of the causative agent and initiation of supportive therapy. However, clinicians should advise patients with rhinitis medicamentosa against reusing topical decongestants, even for short durations, because rebound congestion may recur rapidly with repeated exposure.

The recovery timeline depends on the treatment approach used. Subjective symptoms of rebound congestion may resolve within 48 hours when intranasal corticosteroids are initiated alongside discontinuation of the decongestant, whereas resolution may take longer than one week with placebo. In contrast, objective mucosal abnormalities, such as edema and inflammation, may take longer to resolve, often requiring 7 to 14 days of treatment. These findings suggest that although acute withdrawal symptoms may resolve relatively quickly, full mucosal recovery and optimal symptom management might necessitate a longer treatment period.

For patients with chronic rhinitis treated with intranasal corticosteroids, achieving maximum therapeutic benefit may take several weeks. However, initial clinical improvement is often seen within the first day of treatment. These findings indicate that although acute withdrawal symptoms may resolve relatively quickly, full mucosal recovery and optimal symptom management might necessitate a longer treatment period.

## Deterrence and Patient Education

Patients should be educated on the potential adverse effects of prolonged or inappropriate use of intranasal topical decongestants, ideally before initiation of therapy. A subdural hematoma develops from the accumulation of blood in the plane between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane (see Image. Subdural Hematoma Tentorium). An accurate understanding of subdural hematoma depends on knowledge of the neuroanatomical coverings of the brain. The brain is composed of interconnected neurons and supporting connective tissue that are highly susceptible to injury without adequate protection. Protection begins with the scalp and bony skull and continues internally with the meninges, which consist of 3 distinct layers.

[그림/Figure] Figure 1 Subdural Hematoma Tentorium. Rupture of thin-walled bridging veins under opposing mechanical forces releases blood into the subdural space, resulting in a subdural hematoma. Contributed by S Dulebohn, MD

[그림/Figure] Figure 2 Subdural Hematoma. A subdural hematoma develops from the accumulation of blood beneath the dura mater, one of the protective layers covering the brain tissue under the calvarium. Contributed by S Dulebohn, MD

Along the inner surface of the skull, the dura mater forms a dense layer and adheres to the periosteum through its outer surface, while facing the arachnoid mater through its inner surface. The arachnoid mater lies beneath the dura as the middle meningeal layer. The innermost meningeal layer is the pia mater. Bridging veins cross the plane between the dura and the arachnoid to drain blood coming from the brain into the dural venous system. Rupture of these thin-walled bridging veins under opposing mechanical forces releases blood into the subdural space, resulting in a subdural hematoma.

A larger potential space between the dura mater and the brain, commonly observed in the developing or aging brain due to cerebral volume loss, allows cerebrospinal fluid to occupy a greater volume within the spaces between the bridging veins. This expansion stretches the veins and increases vulnerability to rupture. Small extravasations may resolve spontaneously, whereas larger hemorrhages expand the subdural space, promote progressive blood layering around the brain, create mass effect, and ultimately precipitate herniation of cerebral structures.

The term subdural hematoma covers biologically distinct entities that share a location but not a mechanism. Acute subdural hematoma usually follows trauma and behaves as an expanding extra-axial mass coupled to primary parenchymal injury. Chronic subdural hematoma is an inflammatory neomembrane disease sustained by angiogenesis, hyperfibrinolysis, and recurrent microhemorrhage. This distinction matters because acute lesions are managed with an emphasis on the risk of imminent herniation, whereas chronic lesions are managed with a focus on symptom progression, recurrence, and frailty-sensitive recovery.

The usual temporal framework remains clinically useful. An acute subdural hematoma is blood imaged within the first 72 hours after injury. Subacute lesions usually occupy a 3- to 21-day interval. Chronic lesions are typically defined after 3 weeks, although mixed-density and acute-on-chronic collections show that radiographic appearance reflects repeated bleeding episodes. A small acute clot can therefore evolve into a chronic, membrane-lined collection, while a chronic hematoma can acquire hyperdense acute components after interval rebleeding.

The disease burden is rising. Population aging, cerebral atrophy, higher fall frequency, and widespread antithrombotic exposure have expanded the pool of patients at risk for both traumatic acute lesions and nonacute recurrent collections. Contemporary United States data estimate chronic subdural hematoma incidence at 17.3 per 100,000 persons per year, with incidence exceeding 350 per 100,000 in men aged 85 years or older. Chronic subdural hematoma is projected to become the most common cranial neurosurgical disease by 2030 if current demographic trends persist. In parallel, older adults now represent a large share of acute subdural hematoma presentations and often arrive with baseline frailty, anticoagulant use, or both, which alters operative risk, postoperative recovery, and long-term mortality.

## Treatment / Management

Immediate Medical Management

Acute management of subdural hematomas begins with securing the airway when consciousness is depressed or when airway protection is unreliable. Prompt correction of hypoxemia, avoidance of hypotension, elevation of the head of the bed, and immediate treatment of active seizures remain essential, as these interventions limit secondary ischemic injury while operative decisions progress. Hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline should be initiated in the presence of clinical or radiographic signs of herniation; however, this approach functions as a temporary bridge rather than a definitive alternative to surgical evacuation. Following stabilization, ventilation should return to normocapnia. Brief hyperventilation may serve as a rescue intervention in cases of impending herniation.

In vitamin K antagonist-associated intracranial hemorrhage, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K is the standard strategy because it corrects the international normalized ratio rapidly and with less volume than plasma. Idarucizumab is a reasonable reversal agent for dabigatran. Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors, where available, while 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate remains widely used when andexanet is unavailable or impractical. Thrombocytopenia should be corrected, especially when craniotomy or burr-hole drainage is planned. Antiplatelet reversal is less certain. Routine platelet transfusion for all antiplatelet-exposed patients is not supported by high-quality evidence; practice should be individualized based on platelet count, operative urgency, and recent drug exposure.

Nonoperative Management

Observation is appropriate for selected acute subdural hematomas that are small, produce limited mass effect, and occur in patients with preserved or rapidly stabilizing neurologic examinations. Observation requires serial neurologic assessment, repeat imaging, and rescue surgery if deterioration occurs. Current observational data from CENTER-TBI suggest that, in patients in genuine clinical equipoise, routine early surgery does not automatically improve functional outcomes, supporting conservative management in patients with modest lesions and a stable exam.

Conservative management also has a role in chronic subdural hematoma. Patients with no or only mild symptoms, limited mass effect, high operative risk, or clear spontaneous radiographic regression can be managed without immediate surgery if follow-up is dependable and crossover to surgery criteria are followed. Crossover remains common, so observation should be presented as active surveillance.

Adjunctive pharmacotherapy remains unsettled. Atorvastatin demonstrated reductions in hematoma volume and lower rates of surgical conversion in a randomized trial from China, and meta-analytic data remain supportive; however, external validity across broader populations remains uncertain. Tranexamic acid has shown promising signals of both recurrence and resolution, yet methodological heterogeneity and unresolved questions about thrombotic safety preclude its routine adoption as standard care. The clearest negative signal concerns corticosteroids. Dexamethasone worsened overall clinical outcomes in Dex-CSDH and failed noninferiority against burr-hole drainage in DECSA, with more complications and later rescue surgery. Routine corticosteroid treatment for symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma should therefore be avoided.

Surgical Indications

In acute subdural hematoma, evacuation is recommended when either of the following is present, regardless of Glasgow Coma Scale score: hematoma thickness greater than 10 mm, or midline shift greater than 5 mm on CT. A comatose patient, defined as a Glasgow Coma Scale score less than 9, with a smaller acute subdural hematoma should also undergo evacuation if any of the following are present: a decline in Glasgow Coma Scale score by 2 or more points between injury and hospital assessment, asymmetric or fixed dilated pupils, or intracranial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg. Once the indication is established, surgery should proceed as soon as possible.

In chronic subdural hematoma, the 2026 guidelines from the UK recommend that surgery be performed in patients with symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma. Surgery should also be considered in patients with minimal or no symptoms when imaging demonstrates a large-volume hematoma with mass effect, eg, a midline shift greater than 5 mm.

Surgical Techniques for Acute Subdural Hematoma

Craniotomy remains the standard evacuation technique for most surgically treated acute subdural hematomas because it allows rapid removal of the clot and hemostasis. The central intraoperative question is whether the bone flap can be safely replaced. When the brain is swollen, and replacement would recreate dangerous intracranial hypertension, decompressive craniectomy with duraplasty is appropriate. When swelling is modest and hemostasis is secure, a craniotomy with bone flap replacement avoids the need for a later cranioplasty.

The RESCUE-ASDH randomized trial established that primary decompressive craniectomy and craniotomy produce similar disability and quality-of-life outcomes at 12 months in patients for whom both techniques were feasible. Additional cranial surgery was more common after craniotomy, while wound complications were more frequent after decompressive craniectomy. Contemporary observational and meta-analytic studies support individualized selection and do not show consistent overall functional superiority of one technique across all patients.

Surgical Techniques for Chronic Subdural Hematoma

Burr-hole evacuation with closed-system drainage remains the reference operation for symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma because it combines high symptom relief with low invasiveness. Clinicians may use 1 or 2 burr holes. Twist-drill craniostomy is useful in selected frail patients with liquefied nonseptated collections. Craniotomy or mini-craniotomy is usually reserved for organized, solid, heavily septated, recurrent, or calcified hematomas where simple drainage is unlikely to succeed.

Postoperative drainage represents one of the most well-supported evidence-based interventions in the management of subdural hematoma. A randomized trial demonstrated that placement of a subdural drain following burr-hole evacuation reduced recurrence rates and improved survival compared with no drainage. Subsequent meta-analyses have confirmed that closed-system drainage plays a critical role in achieving durable surgical success. Evidence supports the use of both subdural and subgaleal closed drainage systems.

Intraoperative irrigation also influences outcomes. The FINISH randomized trial showed that omitting irrigation failed to demonstrate noninferiority and was associated with higher reoperation rates, supporting continued use of irrigation during standard burr-hole evacuation in most patients. In the absence of anatomical constraints or patient instability, burr-hole washout combined with postoperative closed drainage remains the most evidence-based standard surgical approach.

Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization

Three randomized trials have evaluated embolization in the management of nonacute or chronic subdural hematoma, demonstrating a reduction in treatment failure or need for reoperation in selected populations. EMBOLISE and STEM showed benefits for recurrence-related endpoints, whereas MAGIC-MT did not significantly reduce the primary 90-day symptomatic recurrence or progression outcome, although it reported fewer serious adverse events. Meta-analyses of randomized data suggest that middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) reduces the risk of symptomatic progression or recurrence; however, this effect has not reached statistical significance overall and should be interpreted in light of heterogeneity in background treatments and endpoint definitions.

Current evidence supports a selective role for embolization. This approach offers value as an adjunct following surgical evacuation in patients at high risk for recurrence, in cases of recurrent chronic subdural hematoma, and as a primary option in mildly symptomatic nonacute disease when rapid decompression remains unnecessary. Embolization should not replace surgical evacuation in patients with significant mass effect, progressive neurological deficits, or impaired consciousness, as the technique does not provide immediate decompression. Guidelines from the United Kingdom, published in 2026, advise against the routine use of MMAE in the management of chronic subdural hematoma.

Adjunctive Perioperative Management

Seizure management should be individualized to lesion type and associated cortical injury. For moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, current Neurocritical Care Society guidance does not demonstrate a clear functional advantage for universal prophylaxis; however, when prophylaxis is used, levetiracetam is generally favored over phenytoin or fosphenytoin, and short courses of 7 days or less are preferred. Routine prolonged prophylaxis after uncomplicated chronic subdural drainage is not evidence-based.

Resumption of antithrombotic therapy requires individualized risk balancing. The key prerequisites are stable hemostasis, radiographic stability when clinically indicated, and a clear understanding of the patient’s thromboembolic risk if therapy remains withheld. The guidelines suggest initiating venous thromboembolism chemoprophylaxis 24 to 48 hours after surgery and 6 hours after drain removal.

Pediatric Management

In pediatric patients, immediate management begins with airway protection, respiratory support, and circulatory stabilization under the direction of the critical care team. After stabilization and close monitoring, clinicians should establish a comprehensive care plan that includes neurosurgical and neurological consultations to determine injury severity and anticipate short- and long-term outcomes.

Conservative, nonsurgical management may be appropriate for subacute and chronic subdural hematomas when blood accumulation has not progressed sufficiently to compress the brain or brainstem. In contrast, a rapidly expanding subdural hematoma or one causing signs of increased intracranial pressure, eg, hypertension, bradycardia with irregular respirations, demands urgent surgical evacuation to preserve vital functions. Concurrently, clinicians should initiate immediate medical management, including sedation, neuromuscular blockade when indicated, moderate hyperventilation targeting a PaCO2 of 32 to 36 mm Hg, maintenance of SpO2 above 95%, head elevation, and avoidance of hyperthermia. Infusion of hypertonic saline or mannitol helps reduce intracranial pressure by inducing osmotic shifts within the brain and transiently modifying cerebral blood flow rheology, respectively.

text:
## Prognosis

Advanced age, low admission Glasgow Coma Scale score, nonreactive pupils, hypotension, and associated intracranial injuries consistently predict poor outcome. In older surgical patients, the aggregate data remain sobering. Mortality approaches one-half by follow-up, and poor functional outcome is common, although selected individuals with preserved pupils, limited comorbidity, and rapid decompression can still recover meaningful independence. The Subdural Hematoma in the Elderly score predicts 30-day mortality using variables available at presentation. These prognostic tools are useful for communication and benchmarking. However, these tools should not be used to deny surgery to a patient with a clearly reversible compressive syndrome.

The short-term prognosis is generally better in chronic subdural hematoma than in acute, but the long-term picture is less benign than the surgical series alone implies. Operative cohorts often report good neurologic recovery, as exemplified by the Swiss multicenter study, in which 81% achieved a good postoperative outcome, and in-hospital mortality was 4%. Population-level data tell a broader story. In the recent United States cohort, 30-day mortality was 9.4%, and 1-year mortality reached 32.9%, reflecting the contribution of frailty, falls, comorbidity, and loss of independence after the hematoma episode.

Pediatric Prognosis

The prognosis of children affected by subdural hematoma is widely variable and depends on the extent of the intracranial injury. Many cases of subdural hematoma, either traumatic or abusive, remain undetected. However, many children live with severe neurological deficits, including seizures, neurodevelopmental delay with static encephalopathy, because of severe, devastating neurological injury.

text:
## Complications

The most serious early complication of acute subdural hematoma involves secondary brain injury resulting from ongoing compression. Herniation, cerebral infarction due to reduced perfusion, seizures, and delayed hematoma expansion may occur before or after definitive treatment. Postoperative complications include rebleeding, persistent mass effect, hydrocephalus in severe injury patterns, wound breakdown, and infection. Decompressive craniectomy introduces additional long-term risks, including syndrome of the trephined and complications related to subsequent cranioplasty, while craniotomy carries an increased likelihood of requiring secondary decompression when postoperative cerebral swelling exceeds intraoperative expectations.

In chronic subdural hematoma, recurrence represents the primary complication. Despite advances in surgical techniques and drainage strategies, repeat intervention remains necessary in a substantial subset of patients. Recurrence risk depends on factors, eg, membrane activity, imaging characteristics, bilateral involvement, residual cavity size, and degree of postoperative brain reexpansion. Omission of postoperative drainage significantly increases this risk. Additional complications include acute postoperative hemorrhage, pneumocephalus, seizures, delirium, empyema, and incomplete neurologic recovery when presenting symptoms do not fully originate from the hematoma.

Embolization introduces a distinct complication profile. Clinical trials demonstrate an acceptable overall safety profile; however, risks include disabling stroke, cranial nerve ischemia, vascular access complications, and nontarget embolization. Clinicians should counsel patients that reduced recurrence risk may be accompanied by a small but meaningful endovascular risk.

Pediatric Complications

Subdural hematoma can lead to a wide range of acute and long-term complications. In the acute phase, ongoing bleeding and cerebral edema may cause rising intracranial pressure, herniation, and potentially fatal neurologic decline if not recognized and managed promptly. These risks are higher when additional traumatic brain injuries (eg, diffuse axonal injury or parenchymal contusions) are present. Hydrocephalus is another important complication in pediatric traumatic brain injury. Children with subdural hematoma are particularly vulnerable and may require CSF diversion and continued neurosurgical follow-up.

Posttraumatic seizures are also common, especially in children with severe injuries, depressed mental status, or intracranial hemorrhage. Seizures may occur early (within the first week following injury) or later in recovery and can contribute to secondary injury and long-term epilepsy. Some patients develop chronic or acute-on-chronic subdural collections after the initial event, particularly those with coagulopathies, bleeding diathesis, or repeated trauma. These may present weeks to months later with new neurologic symptoms, seizures, or recurrent signs of increased intracranial pressure.

In the long term, survivors (especially infants and young children with abusive head trauma) may experience persistent neurocognitive, behavioral, visual, and motor impairments, including developmental delay, spasticity, learning difficulties, and static encephalopathy. These outcomes highlight the importance of early rehabilitation, coordinated follow-up, and ongoing interprofessional support for patients and their families.

## Deterrence and Patient Education

Effective prevention of subdural hematoma centers on reducing modifiable risk factors and equipping patients and caregivers to recognize early signs of deterioration. Fall prevention is the highest-yield intervention in older adults, and should include balance training, home hazard modification, vision correction, and review of sedating or hypotensive medications. Antithrombotic management requires explicit counseling on indication, dosing, adherence, and bleeding risk, with individualized decisions on initiation, interruption, and resumption based on thromboembolic risk and hematoma status. Patients with alcohol use disorder should receive targeted counseling and referral for treatment, as chronic alcohol exposure increases fall risk and impairs coagulation.

Patient education must emphasize the delayed presentation of chronic subdural hematoma, with clear instructions to seek urgent care for new or worsening headache, gait instability, cognitive decline, focal deficits, or altered consciousness. After treatment, patients and families should understand the recurrence risk, the need for follow-up imaging when indicated, and activity guidance, including a gradual return to baseline function and the avoidance of high-risk activities until stability is confirmed. Structured discharge instructions and caregiver engagement improve adherence and facilitate early detection of complications, which directly influences outcomes.

Deterrence and Patient Education in Pediatric Patients

Deterrence and patient education are key to reducing the risk of subdural hematoma, especially in infants and young children. Caregivers should receive clear guidance on normal infant crying and safe soothing techniques, with an emphasis that shaking an infant can cause severe brain injury or death. Anticipatory guidance at well-child visits and community programs that address caregiver stress and support needs are important in preventing abusive head trauma. Clinicians should also reinforce safe sleep and handling practices, proper car seat use, and strategies to reduce the risk of fall-related injuries.

For families of children who have already sustained a subdural hematoma, education should focus on recognizing signs of worsening neurologic status (eg, seizures, persistent vomiting, or changes in behavior) and when to seek urgent care. Caregivers should understand the need for follow-up with neurosurgery, neurology, and rehabilitation services, adherence to medications, and early developmental support when indicated. When abusive head trauma is involved, social workers and child protection teams play a central role in ensuring safety and coordinating ongoing services.

## Introduction

The syndrome of hemolysis with a microangiopathic blood smear, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets in pregnant and postpartum patients is more commonly known by the acronym HELLP syndrome. It may represent a complication or progression of severe preeclampsia; however, this relationship has been challenged by recent evidence that they may be separate disorders as preceding hypertension or proteinuria is absent in at least 15 to 20% of patients with HELLP syndrome. A previous history of preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome can lead to recurrence in subsequent pregnancies.

Multiparity and age may contribute to increased risk. Genetic association for increased predisposition for HELLP syndrome has been noted. It has been recently reported that patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy have an increased risk for preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

## Treatment / Management

Medical management is mainly supportive. These patients may need ventilator support, vasopressor support, pain control, monitoring of volume status, and nutritional support. As these patients can rapidly deteriorate, they are best managed at tertiary care centers with appropriate levels of maternal and neonatal intensive care units. Consideration should be given to transferring them immediately after stabilization from the hospitals where such medical attention can not be provided.

The first step in managing these seriously ill patients is to stabilize them and assess fetal status with a nonstress test and ultrasound examination for a biophysical profile.

Intensivist, hepatologist, nephrologist, hematologist, surgical, gynecologist, and neonatologist consultations should be considered promptly to comanage them.

Patients with severe hypertension should be immediately started on intravenous labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine.

Patients with severe right upper quadrant or epigastric pain and elevated liver function tests should be evaluated promptly with a bedside ultrasound to rule out liver rupture, fulminant liver failure, or hepatic bleeding and may need to be confirmed with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging(MRI). Surgical intervention, including liver transplantation, may be needed if there is evidence of liver rupture. Less invasive percutaneous embolization of the hepatic arteries may be considered in stable patients.

Management is mainly supportive in patients with DIC, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory failure, and acute kidney injury and should be stabilized according to the clinical guidelines.

Massive transfusions may be required. Consider patients for red cell transfusion if hemoglobin is <7gm/dl or if the patient has ecchymosis, severe hematuria, or suspected placental abruption. All actively bleeding patients with any degree of thrombocytopenia should be transfused with platelets. Patients with coexisting DIC may need fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate.

Patients with HELLP syndrome and coexisting TTP will benefit from therapeutic plasma exchange.

Patients should be referred immediately to a gynecologist to consider prompt delivery as it is the only effective treatment. Betamethasone administration is recommended for fetal lung maturity when the patient presents at <34 weeks of gestation. Magnesium sulfate should be initiated at the time of admission to prevent maternal seizures and neuroprotective effects on the fetus/neonate. In two large double-blind, randomized trials, there was no proven benefit to administering dexamethasone in patients with HELLP syndrome as it did not improve maternal or perinatal/infant outcomes.

## Prognosis

HELLP syndrome is a life-threatening condition. The mortality rate of women with HELLP syndrome is 0%-24%, with a perinatal death rate of up to 37%. Maternal death occurs due to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage, or acute renal failure. DIC occurs in 15% to 62.5% of the cases. Placental abruption occurs in 11% to 25% of women with HELLP syndrome. Postpartum hemorrhage occurs in 12.5% to 40% and acute renal failure in 36% to 50% of the cases. Poor perinatal prognosis is because of placental abruption, intrauterine hypoxia, asphyxia, prematurity, and low birth weight.

Patients with HELLP syndrome have a 19% to 27% risk of developing HELLP syndrome in subsequent pregnancies. Recurrent cases occur in the latter part of the gestation period and are less severe after two episodes.

## Complications

HELLP syndrome is a life-threatening condition with high maternal and infant mortality rates. Maternal complications include:

1. Eclampsia
2. Placental abruption
3. Cesarean section
4. DIC
5. Recurrent thrombosis
6. Liver rupture/hematoma
7. Fulminant liver failure
8. Cerebral infarction
9. Cerebral hemorrhage
10. Pulmonary/cerebral edema
11. Cardiovascular instability
12. Acute kidney injury
13. Infection/sepsis
14. retinal detachment
15. severe peripartum bleeding
16. Maternal death

Fetal complications include:

1. Perinatal death
2. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
3. Preterm birth
4. Neonatal thrombocytopenia,leukopenia,neutropenia

text:
## Introduction

Sensory neuropathies refer to a host of diseases that result in loss of sensation throughout the body. Collectively, sensory neuropathies can result from a plethora of conditions. These sensory neuropathies may be subdivided into small fiber pain-dominant and large fiber ataxia-predominant pathologies.

Appropriate treatment and management are determined by sensory neuropathy classification, which is based on nerve size and degree of myelination. When assessing small fiber neuropathies, the small somatic Aδ and small unmyelinated C fibers are of particular interest. These fibers transmit noxious and thermal signals and regulate preganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic function via the Aδ fibers and postganglionic autonomic function via the C fibers. Disruption of the normal physiological state of these fibers typically results in burning and shooting pain with paresthesia.

In contrast, large fiber neuropathies result from attenuating Aβ fibers, which regulate the proprioceptive signals of vibration and touch. Grossly speaking, patients with sensory ataxia likely possess deformation to the dorsal columns of the spinal cord as well as the dorsal root ganglia. Although ataxia is pathognomonic for large-fiber sensory neuropathy, subsequent damage to smaller fibers may occur. As such, some diseases may yield mixed etiology polyneuropathies, composed of small and large fibers (eg, diabetes mellitus), and present some of the most significant public health burdens in modern-day medicine.

Classic clinical findings include complaints of "pins and needles" and "electricity" in the affected extremities, which follow a stocking-glove pattern. Evaluation of sensory neuropathy primarily revolves around neurophysiological examination and dermatopathological studies such as skin biopsy, the current validated gold standard for diagnosing small fiber neuropathy. Guidelines on specific treatment modalities for sensory neuropathies have not been defined. The majority of the data regarding treatments are based on expert opinions, along with well-constructed research. Treatments include injection of intravenous immunoglobulins, methotrexate, corticosteroids, infliximab, plasma exchange, and various oral topical medications, depending on the etiology. This activity reviews the evaluation and management of patients with sensory neuropathies.
